title: How Does Adult Attachment Style Relate to Inflammation?
abstract: Anxious and avoidant attachment style in adulthood has been predictive of higher levels of stress, and poor physical and mental health, while secure attachment style serves as a protective factor (e.g., Mikulincer & Shaver, 2012; Pietromonaco, Uchino, & Schetter, 2013). Stress can induce elevated inflammation, a biological risk for physical and mental health (Nusslock & Miller, 2016). The two literatures point to the possibility of a relationship between attachment style and inflammation. However, research examining this question is sparse. To address the literature gap, we explored the relations of several attachment dimensions with inflammation. We hypothesized that anxious and avoidant attachment would associate with higher inflammation while secure attachment would associate with lower inflammation. Method: We recruited 210 older adolescents (M age = 18.6 years; range = 18-19 years) from the Chicago and Los Angeles metropolitan areas. Blood was collected via antecubital venipuncture and assayed for the inflammatory proteins of the interleukin class (IL-6, -8, -10), tumor necrosis-alpha, and C-reactive protein. Inflammatory dynamic was indexed by an inflammation composite score (ICS) from the markers based on the procedure by Nusslock et al. (2019). Measures of attachment quality included the Experience in Close Relationships Questionnaire (Fraley, Waller, & Brennan, 2000) and the Measurement of Attachment Quality (Carver, 1997). Results: In a single linear model, we entered each attachment style as a predictor of the ICS, covarying for the effects of variables known to account for variation in the immune response (e.g., sex, BMI, recent illness). Anxious, avoidant, and secure attachment style did not account for significant variation in the ICS (Mean β = |.07|, ps ≥ .13). Conclusions: Collectively, these results extend our understanding of the cross-sectional relations between adult attachment style and inflammatory activity and partially align with the results of related inquiries (Kidd et al., 2014).
